title: Backend for Frontend (BFF)
description: Learn the Backend for Frontend pattern for building tailored APIs for different client types.

data.text: The Backend for Frontend (BFF) pattern, pioneered by Netflix and SoundCloud, creates a custom backend API for each client type (web, mobile, tablet). This avoids over-fetching and provides the exact data shape each client needs.
Generic APIs often force clients to make multiple calls or fetch unnecessary data. A BFF aggregates and shapes data specifically for one client type, reducing round-trips and improving performance.

data.title: BFF Benefits
items: Provides data in the exact shape the client needs
Hides backend complexity from frontend teams

data.text: An API Gateway is a generic entry point for all clients. A BFF is a custom API built specifically for one client type. BFFs often sit behind the API Gateway, which routes requests to the appropriate BFF.

data.title: GraphQL as BFF
data.text: GraphQL servers are often used as BFFs because they let clients request exactly the data they need. Many companies use Apollo Server as a BFF aggregating multiple downstream services.

items.question: How many BFFs should I have?
items.answer: One per client type. If you have web, mobile, and tablet clients, you might have three BFFs. Avoid creating a BFF per team or feature.

items.question: Can BFFs become a monolith?
items.answer: Yes, if you are not careful. Keep BFFs small and focused. Use GraphQL or lightweight frameworks to avoid BFF bloat.

items.question: Should BFFs share code?
items.answer: Share common utilities like authentication and error handling, but keep the data aggregation logic separate for each client type.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: BFF provides a custom API for each client type
GraphQL is a natural fit for BFF
data.takeaway: Use BFF when generic APIs cause client-side performance or complexity problems.
